## 0. What this notebook does

88 candidate binders against the RcaT toxin, pooled and sequenced under
several conditions (`config/samples_template.tsv`). RcaT kills the cell unless
something blocks it, so a binder's relative abundance after selection
reflects how well it protects the cell.

Conditions:

- `plasmid_library` - the pooled plasmid prep itself, sequenced directly,
  no cells involved at all (Section 2).
- `no_inducer` - grown, plain antibiotic selection only (Section 2-3).
- `library_only_0.1mM` - binder induced, no toxin.
- `toxin_plus_library_0.1mM` - binder induced, toxin present.

`toxin_only` is loaded but not used downstream - why might that be?

This notebook is meant to be worked through together, not just run - each
section ends with something to discuss before moving on.

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)   # readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, purrr
library(scales)      # nice axis labels
setwd("/home/bourn/phd-primer-binder/analysis/") # change yourself
```

## 1. Load data

```{r load-data}
counts_long <- read_tsv("../results/binder_counts.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
samples     <- read_tsv("../config/samples_template.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# A binder with zero reads in a sample is simply absent from binder_counts.tsv -
# fill those in explicitly rather than letting them silently disappear.
counts_long <- counts_long %>%
  complete(binder_id, sample_id = samples$sample_id, fill = list(count = 0)) %>%
  left_join(samples %>% select(sample_id, condition, ara_pct, iptg_mM),
            by = "sample_id")

head(counts_long)
```

```{r wide-matrix}
counts_wide <- counts_long %>%
  select(binder_id, sample_id, count) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sample_id, values_from = count, values_fill = 0)

counts_wide
```

One row per binder, one column per sample - does this match what you
expected from `config/samples_template.tsv`? Anything surprising already?

## 2. Library representation: plasmid pool vs. after growth

`plasmid_library` is the pooled plasmid prep itself - no transformation, no
growth, no selection at all. Comparing it to `no_inducer` (grown, plain
antibiotic selection, nothing induced) tells you whether any skew you see
later already existed in the tube, or only shows up once cells start
growing.

```{r plasmid-library-check}
plasmid_vs_no_inducer <- counts_long %>%
  filter(condition %in% c("plasmid_library", "no_inducer")) %>%
  group_by(sample_id) %>%
  mutate(freq = count / sum(count)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(binder_id, condition, freq) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = freq)

plasmid_vs_no_inducer %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = plasmid_library, y = no_inducer)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number()) +
  labs(x = "Relative frequency: plasmid_library", y = "Relative frequency: no_inducer",
       title = "Library representation: raw plasmid prep vs. after growth") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Does this look like fair representation, or does the library structure
already look skewed before a single cell was even grown?

## 3. QC: sequencing depth and binder detection

```{r qc-depth}
depth <- counts_long %>%
  group_by(sample_id, condition) %>%
  summarise(total_reads = sum(count), n_binders_detected = sum(count > 0), .groups = "drop")

depth %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(sample_id, total_reads), y = total_reads, fill = condition)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Total usable read pairs", title = "Sequencing depth per sample") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r qc-table}
depth
```

A sample with much lower depth than the others deserves a second look - what
would you check? (`results/binder_counts_qc.tsv`, if you ran
`count_reads_per_binder.py`, has per-sample unmapped/low-MAPQ/mate-mismatch
counts worth a look too.)

### Library complexity: how evenly is the pool represented?

Every binder's count here is a share of a fixed total - if a handful of
binders dominate, everyone else is squeezed regardless of biology.

```{r library-complexity}
complexity <- counts_long %>%
  group_by(sample_id, condition) %>%
  mutate(sample_total = sum(count)) %>%
  arrange(sample_id, desc(count)) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number(), cum_share = cumsum(count) / sample_total) %>%
  ungroup()

complexity %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rank, y = cum_share, group = sample_id, colour = condition)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.9, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Binders, ranked by abundance (most abundant first)",
       y = "Cumulative share of reads",
       title = "Library complexity per sample",
       subtitle = "A steep early climb to the dashed line (90%) means a handful of binders dominate the pool") +
  theme_minimal()

complexity %>%
  filter(cum_share >= 0.9) %>%
  group_by(sample_id, condition) %>%
  summarise(binders_for_90pct_of_reads = min(rank), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(binders_for_90pct_of_reads)
```

If a handful of binders dominate every sample about equally, is that more
likely a pool-prep problem or a selection effect? (You already have an
answer to that from Section 2.)

### Viability filter: drop binders that don't survive no-inducer selection

```{r viability-filter}
min_no_inducer_reads <- 10  # tune by eye against the dataframe produced

no_inducer_counts <- counts_long %>%
  filter(condition == "no_inducer") %>%
  select(binder_id, no_inducer_count = count)

no_inducer_counts %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = no_inducer_count + 1)) +   # +1 so zero counts survive the log
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey30", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = min_no_inducer_reads + 1,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000),
    labels = scales::comma,
    guide = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE)
  ) +
  labs(x = "no_inducer read count (+1, log10 scale)",
       y = "Number of binders",
       title = "Choosing the viability threshold",
       subtitle = paste("Dashed line: current threshold =", min_no_inducer_reads)) +
  theme_minimal()

dead_binders <- no_inducer_counts %>%
  filter(no_inducer_count < min_no_inducer_reads) %>%
  pull(binder_id)

if (length(dead_binders) > 0) {
  cat(length(dead_binders), " binder(s) dropped as non-viable (no_inducer count < ",
      min_no_inducer_reads, "): ", paste(dead_binders, collapse = ", "), "\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("No binders dropped - all binders survive no-inducer selection above threshold.\n")
}

counts_long <- counts_long %>% filter(!(binder_id %in% dead_binders))
```

### Low-count filter: drop binders too thinly covered overall

The viability filter above only looks at `no_inducer`. What's it missing?

```{r low-count-filter}
min_mean_count <- 5  # tune by eye against the histogram below

mean_counts <- counts_long %>%
  filter(condition != "plasmid_library") %>%  # not part of the downstream comparison
  group_by(binder_id) %>%
  summarise(mean_count = mean(count), .groups = "drop")

mean_counts %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_count + 1)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey30", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = min_mean_count + 1,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000),
    labels = scales::comma,
    guide = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Mean read count across all samples (+1, log10 scale)",
       y = "Number of binders",
       title = "Choosing the low-count filter threshold",
       subtitle = paste("Dashed line: current threshold =", min_mean_count)) +
  theme_minimal()

low_count_binders <- mean_counts %>%
  filter(mean_count < min_mean_count) %>%
  pull(binder_id)

if (length(low_count_binders) > 0) {
  cat(length(low_count_binders), " binder(s) dropped for too few reads overall (mean count < ",
      min_mean_count, "): ", paste(low_count_binders, collapse = ", "), "\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("No binders dropped - all binders average at least ", min_mean_count, " reads across all samples.\n", sep = "")
}

counts_long <- counts_long %>% filter(!(binder_id %in% low_count_binders))
```

Between the viability and low-count filters, how many binders got dropped
in total? Does that feel like a lot, for 88 designed binders?

## 4. Normalisation

Convert each binder's count to its relative frequency within the sample,
with a pseudocount so zero-count binders don't produce `-Inf` on the log
scale.

```{r normalise}
pseudocount <- 1

counts_norm <- counts_long %>%
  group_by(sample_id) %>%
  mutate(
    total_reads = sum(count),
    freq        = (count + pseudocount) / (total_reads + pseudocount * n_distinct(counts_long$binder_id))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

counts_norm %>% select(sample_id, binder_id, count, total_reads, freq) %>% head()
```

Why divide by total reads instead of comparing raw counts directly? What
would raw counts conflate?

## 5. Innate toxicity of overexpression (reference only)

How much does overexpressing each binder cost the cell on its own, with no
toxin present (`library_only_0.1mM` vs. `no_inducer`)? Not used in Section 6 -
context only.

```{r innate-toxicity}
baseline <- counts_norm %>%
  filter(condition == "no_inducer") %>%
  select(binder_id, baseline_freq = freq)

innate_toxicity <- counts_norm %>%
  filter(condition == "library_only_0.1mM") %>%
  left_join(baseline, by = "binder_id") %>%
  mutate(log2FC = log2(freq / baseline_freq))

innate_toxicity %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = binder_id, y = log2FC)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Binder", y = "log2FC vs. no_inducer",
       title = "Innate toxicity of overexpression (no toxin present)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())
```

Does any binder here look costly enough to overexpress that it's worth
remembering if it also shows up near the top of the hit table later?

## 6. Fitness: toxin+library vs. library-only

DiMSum-style fitness, relative to one reference binder instead of a plain
frequency ratio:

```
fitness = log2( (selected / input) / (ref_selected / ref_input) )
```

`input` = `library_only_0.1mM`, `selected` = `toxin_plus_library_0.1mM`. The reference
is a binder you're confident isn't a real hit - look back at Section 3's
plots. What would make a bad choice here? What would make a good one?

```{r choose-reference}
reference_binder <- ""  # <- pick your own and be ready to justify it

reference_counts <- counts_long %>%
  filter(binder_id == reference_binder, condition %in% c("library_only_0.1mM", "toxin_plus_library_0.1mM")) %>%
  select(condition, count) %>%
  deframe()

ref_input    <- reference_counts[["library_only_0.1mM"]]
ref_selected <- reference_counts[["toxin_plus_library_0.1mM"]]
```

```{r key-comparison}
key_comparison <- counts_long %>%
  filter(condition %in% c("library_only_0.1mM", "toxin_plus_library_0.1mM")) %>%
  select(binder_id, condition, count) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = count) %>%
  rename(input = library_only_0.1mM, selected = toxin_plus_library_0.1mM) %>%
  mutate(
    fitness = log2((selected + pseudocount) / (input + pseudocount) /
                   ((ref_selected + pseudocount) / (ref_input + pseudocount)))
  )

key_comparison %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(binder_id, fitness), y = fitness)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Binder", y = "Fitness (relative to reference)",
       title = "Fitness: toxin+library vs. library-only") +
  theme_minimal()
```

What does this formula assume about the reference binder, and what happens
to every other binder's fitness if that assumption is wrong?

## 7. Final ranked hit table

```{r final-hits}
hit_results <- key_comparison %>%
  select(binder_id, fitness) %>%
  arrange(desc(fitness))

hit_results
```

```{r final-plot}
hit_results %>%
  slice_max(fitness, n = 20) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(binder_id, fitness), y = fitness)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Binder", y = "Fitness (relative to reference)",
       title = "Top 20 RcaT binders by protection") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r save-final-table}
write_csv(hit_results, "../results/final_binder_ranking.csv")
```

Does the top of this table look like a clean break from the rest, or a
gradual slope? What would each imply about where to draw a "hit" line?

## 8. Comparison to the published plate-based screen (Sen2 retron)

Our collaborator's plate-based screen of the same binders
(`data/plate_assay_reference_hits.tsv`, filtered to `retron == "Sen2"` -
Eco9 is a different system). Effect size > 1 means blocking/protective,
matching a positive `fitness` here.

Their baseline and ours aren't the same comparison, and they additionally
correct against a GFP control we don't have - so what should you expect
from this correlation, and how would a weak one change your interpretation?

```{r load-plate-reference}
plate_reference <- read_tsv("../data/plate_assay_reference_hits.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  filter(retron == "Sen2") %>%
  transmute(genename, plate_pval = pval, plate_log2_efsize = log2(efsize), plate_hit = hit)

# binder_id carries a naming-scheme prefix the collaborator's gene names
# don't - strip it to the bare name before joining.
binder_name_map <- tibble(binder_id = unique(hit_results$binder_id)) %>%
  mutate(
    genename = binder_id %>%
      str_remove("^rcat-binder-") %>%
      str_remove("^result_") %>%
      str_replace("_result_", "_")
  )

comparison <- hit_results %>%
  left_join(binder_name_map, by = "binder_id") %>%
  left_join(plate_reference, by = "genename") %>%
  filter(!is.na(plate_log2_efsize))

# make your own correlation plot using this df!
# and work out the correlation coefficient!

```

```{r save-comparison-table}
write_csv(comparison, "../results/plate_assay_comparison.csv")
```

A binder missing from `plate_reference` above just wasn't in that dataset -
check `n_binders_matched` against Section 3's viable-binder count. Overall,
would you call this a successful validation of this screen?

## Where to go from here

* The library-complexity check in Section 3 (and the plasmid-library check
  in Section 2) is worth flagging back to whoever built/pooled this
  plasmid library if it shows a skew - a better-normalised pool (e.g.
  qPCR-checked equimolar pooling) fixes the problem at the source.
* No GFP (or other neutral-overexpression) control is included here. Would
  adding one change how you'd compute fitness in Section 6?
